title: Wavetable Oscillator — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Wavetable Oscillator's rich face: four made walks, each testing what its section says about one stored cycle read by one counter, with the fingerprint of the words each was made against. I grow when the entry is enriched again; I never hold the entry's words.

sections.heading: The same object as a loop

verdicts.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — one cycle, two ways.html
verdicts.why: A real test: no filter restores the null at P + d. Recomputed by simulation and in closed form (linear |H| = cos(ω/2), h10 −0.431 dB a trip; allpass phase delay 1.499 at h1, 1.444 at h10, so +0.955 ¢), and it agrees with Synthesis Topologies' face at the whole period and at N + ½. Note: step 4's 'table' is the exact read; a stored table read between samples has a fixed floor of its own, which a clause could say.

pieces.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — one cycle, two ways.html
pieces.title: one cycle, two ways · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **The identity, heard, and where it stops.** A stored cycle read by a counter; the same cycle round a lossless delay loop; the two subtracted, which at a whole-sample period is zero at every sample (checked over 10 s for periods from 40 to 400 and three shapes: 0, exactly). Then the test: one trip a fraction of a sample longer. Rounded, the loop is out of tune (8.6 cents flat at 100.5 samples). A linear step or an allpass gets the pitch right, within 0.05 cents, but the filter acts on every trip, so the loop parts from the table anyway: at 100.5 samples its difference from the exact read is about −15 and −11 dB after ten trips and −4 dB after a thousand. The linear step loses harmonic 10 by 0.43 dB a trip; the allpass keeps its level and slides it 0.96 cents against harmonic 1. Only a whole-sample trip gives the table back. The page never said the filter restores the match; this measures what it costs. It agrees with Synthesis Topologies' face (the challenger's recomputation on its 16-harmonic saw: −14.9 / −2.9 dB, against its −14.5 / −3.2).
pieces.near: Sample for sample they match only when

sections.heading: Why it can only be harmonic

verdicts.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — a bell on the grid.html
verdicts.why: Words only. (a) The caption's 6 dB at P = 137 (8 to under 1 dB) holds at 48 kHz only; at 44.1 kHz the piece shows −4.2. Say 'at 48 kHz' in the caption and in offer 2. (b) In step 4, say the still rows are bit-identical by construction (the read depends on n mod P alone). (c) The moving bend peaks at 1.14, past the engine's own |b| < 1: cap it (b ≤ 0.52) or say so. The finding holds one-to-one: −9.5 to −1.1 dB.

pieces.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — a bell on the grid.html
pieces.title: a bell on the grid · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Loop one cycle of a bell, and test what lands between.** Risset's bell struck; P samples of it cut and read round and round; the read bent; then a fold that lays every trip on the first and keeps what doesn't line up, which is the energy between the loop's harmonics. The bell keeps nearly all of its energy there. The looped cycle and the bent read keep none, by construction: their read depends on n mod P alone, so every trip is the first, bit for bit. The real test is the last row, the page's condition that every trip takes the same time: a bend that moves 37.7 times a second, its peak held at 0.95 so the read stays one-to-one, every trip still exactly P samples, puts energy between the harmonics: at 48 kHz, 6.9 dB under the whole at P = 137 (9.5 dB down at 60 samples, 1.1 dB down at 600; the numbers move with the sample rate). The read has to hold still, not just the trip's length, which is what Three Kinds of Warp's theorem asks: φ(t + T) − φ(t) = 2π at every t.
pieces.near: So one looped cycle cannot sound inharmonic

verdicts.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — position as a second clock.html
verdicts.why: A real test: repeats after 1, 1, 2, never as the rate goes tied, 3/2 or unrelated, and −7.02 dB recomputed (−7.021 over 10 s). Note: step 4's 'where the page's reading predicts' should say 'where the blend's algebra predicts'; the page predicts leaving the grid, not the number.

pieces.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — position as a second clock.html
pieces.title: Position as a second clock · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Staying inside one loop, and where Position leaves it.** Two frames and a Position held; swept slowly, which moves the harmonics' strengths; driven fast, which grows a line either side of every harmonic, as far off as Position's rate. The test drives it at rates tied to the pitch and untied from it. At the pitch itself the sound repeats every trip and nothing lands between. At three halves it repeats every two trips, a series an octave down. At 37.7 Hz or the golden ratio it never repeats, and the share between the harmonics comes out within 0.01 dB of what the blend's own algebra predicts, (d²/2)·mean((B − A)²) over the whole (−7.02 dB at Position 0.5 ± 0.4): the second clock. The 3/2 row misses it (−7.9 dB) because the modulator's square repeats with the trip. The slow sweep doesn't repeat either, strictly; its new lines sit a quarter of a hertz from their harmonics.

verdicts.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — reading between samples.html
verdicts.why: Measures what the page says it hasn't, and the closed-form error over a uniform fractional offset matches: linear and cubic to 0.1 dB, sample-before within 0.6. The asymptotic slopes are 6.02, 12.04 and 18.06 dB a doubling; the piece's 19 is measured before the asymptote and is honest as measured.

pieces.file: Wavetable Oscillator — rich — reading between samples.html
pieces.title: reading between samples · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **The measurement the page says it hasn't made.** The counter lands between two stored samples nearly every time; read there three ways, one at a time: the sample before, a straight line, a curve through four. The test plays each against the exact cycle at the same phases, on a band-limited saw. At 48 kHz, a 2048-sample table at 220 Hz: −37, −67 and −96 dB under the signal. A 256-sample table at 220 Hz: −20, −32 and −36. Each doubling of the table buys about 6, 12 and 19 dB, measured at 880 Hz between 256 and 2048 samples; for small steps the slopes settle to the textbook 6, 12 and 18 (error orders 1, 2, 3). This is the error's energy, not whether it is heard or where in the spectrum it falls.
pieces.near: Reading a fractional sample inside a frame

offers.section: The same object as a loop
offers.what: The page says 'In between, the loop needs a small filter to land between samples.' The piece measured what the filter costs: it gets the pitch right (linear 0.000 cents, allpass 0.011 cents off fs/(P+d) at P + d = 100.5) but never restores the match, because it acts on every trip. On a 40-harmonic saw at 100.5 samples, the loop's difference from the exact read is −14.9 dB (linear) and −11.3 dB (allpass) at trip 10, −8.9 and −7.1 at trip 100, −3.6 and −3.7 at trip 1000; the linear step loses harmonic 10 by 0.431 dB a trip, the allpass slides it +0.955 cents against harmonic 1. Suggested: 'In between, the loop needs a small filter to land between samples, and the filter acts on every trip: the pitch comes out right, but the loop is no longer the table.'

offers.section: Why it can only be harmonic
offers.what: The page says 'Bend it or distort it: as long as every trip still takes the same time, energy moves among the harmonics and nothing lands between them.' The piece shows that condition is needed but not enough. A still bend puts nothing between (every trip identical to the first, bit for bit, by construction). A bend that itself moves, 37.7 times a second, its peak held at 0.95 so the read stays one-to-one, with every trip still exactly P samples, puts energy between: at 48 kHz, −9.5 dB under the whole at P = 60, −6.9 at 137, −4.5 at 240, −1.1 at 600 (folded over a second of trips). Suggested: 'as long as every trip takes the same time and is read the same way'. That brings the sentence back to the theorem it cites, Three Kinds of Warp's φ(t + T) − φ(t) = 2π for every t; the next paragraph's 'one fixed cycle' already implies it.

The page says 'Reading a fractional sample inside a frame has not been measured here yet.' The piece measures it: each reader against the exact cycle at the same phases, on a band-limited saw, error energy under the signal at 48 kHz. 2048-sample table at 220 Hz: sample-before −37.4 dB, linear −67.1, cubic (Catmull-Rom) −96.2. 256-sample table at 220 Hz: −19.5, −31.7, −36.0. 2048 at 55 Hz (436 harmonics): −31.5, −49.2, −62.1. Each doubling of the table buys about 6, 12 and 19 dB (at 880 Hz). Suggested: replace the sentence with one line of these numbers and a pointer to the piece, saying it measures error energy, not audibility.

Two bullets may be out of date, found by reading as well as by the pieces. 'Hear the identity … Until that exists the identity on this page is argued, not heard': the one-cycle-two-ways piece makes it heard, so once Loudon approves that section the bullet could be marked met. 'The FM question … One of those lines needs its scope stated': [[FM Synthesis]] (line 64) already answers it, 'the ratio is the scope: whole numbers keep the series, anything else leaves it'. The Position piece shows the same scope for Position: driven at the pitch it repeats every trip, at 3/2 every two trips, at 37.7 Hz or the golden ratio never, with −7.02 dB between the harmonics, as the blend's own algebra, (d²/2)·mean((B − A)²) over the whole, predicts. Suggested: point the FM bullet at FM Synthesis's answer.
